dataset.name: Plant Characteristics, Porewater, Gas Flux, and Soil Biogeochemistry at Council Road Site Mile Marker 71, Seward Peninsula, Alaska, 2023
description: Data collected at Council, AK (64°51’35.0”N 163°41’59.1”W) during a summer campaign in 2023. Water data consists of soil porewater collected by centrifuging soil cores and also by field collection with porewater samplers (rhizons). Gas data consists of CO2, CH4 and N2O surface soil fluxes measured with a portable FTIR analyzer. Plant and root data consists of biomass, root length, diameter and mass. Soil data consists of total C and N. Air, water and soil samples span two main locations: a thermokarst wetland and an upland tussock. The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic), was a research effort to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy's Office of Biological and Environmental Research.

The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska. Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy's Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

This dataset was generated to broadly address the following research question: how will climate change (i.e., thawing permafrost, landscape change) alter the ecosystem flux (sink versus source) of important greenhouse gases such as CO2, CH4 and N2O?
Description of the contents of this data package: This dataset contains 5 different individual .csv files containing plant, soil, water and gas data. No software is needed to utilize them.
PFTCover: Plant functional type ground cover in 1x1 meter plots.
SoilCores: Solidphase and porewater phase soil biogeochemical variables
PlantData: Above and belowground plant traits.
FieldPorewater: Field collected porewater biogeochemical variables

Methods
Study Site and Sampling Scheme
The field campaign was conducted from August 30th to September 4th 2023 near Council, AK (64°51’35.0”N 163°41’59.1”W) (Figure 1) as part of the Next Generation Ecosystem Experiment in the Arctic (NGEE Arctic) project (https://ngee-arctic.ornl.gov/). This continental site was characterized as a discontinuous permafrost region with lowland thermokarst wetlands and adjacent upland tussock tundra (Figure 1). Vegetation in the lowland thermokarst wetlands was primarily colonized by aerenchymous graminoids while the upland tundra consisted of a moist acidic tussock tundra community containing a heterogeneous mixture of bryophyte, lichen, graminoids, forbs, and dwarf deciduous and evergreen shrubs (Yang et al. 2021). Our sampling scheme was designed to pair soil, plant, porewater, and GHG flux measurements across these two adjacent landscape positions, as well as across differing PFTs within the upland tussock community (the lowland thermokarst wetland was dominated by only one PFT). We collected data from eight total plots: four in lowland thermokarst wetlands and four in adjacent upland tussock tundra (Figure 1), hereafter referred to as lowland and upland. Within each selected location, a 1-m × 1-m plot with nine 33-cm × 33-cm subplots were designated for plant, soil, porewater, and GHG flux sampling.
Fig. 1 Map of the study site (Google Earth) on the Seward Peninsula near Council, AK at Mile Marker 71 along the Nome-Council Highway. Panel (a) indicates the four lowland and four upland 1-m × 1-m plot locations; (b) shows the location of our intensive field site on the Seward Peninsula; and (c) is an image of the thermokarst lowland versus upland tussock tundra transition (pale green graminoids dominate the thermokarst compared to darker, low-statured shrubs in the upland).
Vegetation PFT Survey
At each plot, the percentage (%) aboveground absolute cover of PFTs was visually quantified within each of the nine 33-cm × 33-cm subplots (i.e., nine subplots in each 1-m × 1-m plot). Cover of bryophyte, lichen, forbs, graminoids, evergreen shrubs, deciduous shrub, bare ground, and standing water were quantified. Species were assigned to PFTs according to Sulman et al. 2021. Absolute cover was then converted to relative cover. In the lowlands, plots were dominated by Carex aquatilis and Eriophorum species. In the uplands, graminoids were primarily tussock-forming sedge, Eriophorum vaginatum, while bryophytes consisted mainly of Sphagnum mosses, with mixtures of Hylocomnium and Pleurozium. Lichen was mostly Cladonia and Thamnolia. Forbs were primarily Rubus chamaemorus. Evergreen shrubs were mixtures of Vaccinium vitis-idaea and Rhododendron tomemtosum, while deciduous shrubs were primarily Vaccinium uliginosum.
Ecosystem GHG Fluxes
Measurement Procedure
Ecosystem gas fluxes (CO2, CH4, N2O and NH3) were measured following PFT surveys. We used the closed-chamber approach in which a 30-cm × 30-cm × 30-cm semi-transparent (i.e., ~67% light transmission) chamber constructed of PVC and polyethylene sheeting was gently placed over vegetation, onto the 33-cm × 33-cm subplot tundra surface. The plastic sheeting edges were sealed to the ground by gently placing a heavy metal chain around the chamber. The flux chamber was connected to a portable Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) gas analyzer (Gasmet Technologies, GT5000) outfitted with gas impermeable tubing. A moisture-removal column (Drierite Co., Lab Gas Drying Unit) was also connected in series due to the wet conditions present at our field site. For each flux measurement, GHG concentrations were recorded every 5 s for ~58 min. Flux values (µmol m-2 s-1) were calculated using the following equation:
Soil GHG Flux= ∆c/∆t V/S Pa/RT
where c is the mole fraction of CO2, CH4, or N2O in µmol mol-1, t is the observation time in s, V is the total volume in m3 of the closed system, S is the surface area in m2 within the flux chamber, Pa is the atmospheric pressure in Pa inside the gas analyzer, R is the universal gas constant (J K-1 mol-1 ), and T is the surface soil temperature in °K. A linear fit was applied to calculate Δc/Δt using Excel. The average R2 across all measurements was 0.83 indicating stable micrometeorological conditions during measurements. We collected light measurements at all 8 plots using the semi-transparent chamber. Five subplot fluxes were measured in each upland plot while 2 subplot fluxes were measured in the lowlands. We also collected one dark measurement in the middle of each plot by placing an opaque tarp over the semi-transparent flux chamber. In total, we report 24 upland fluxes and 12 lowland fluxes. Positive fluxes denote net flow of the gas into the atmosphere while negative fluxes denote the net flow of the gas into the plant-soil system.
Calculation of Ecosystem Gas Exchange
The dark CO2 measurements quantified ecosystem respiration (Reco) and included both soil and plant respiration. The light CO2 measurements quantified net ecosystem exchange (NEE), representing the balance between Reco and gross primary productivity (GPP). GPP was calculated by subtracting Reco (i.e., dark measurements) from NEE (i.e., light measurements) to determine total CO2 uptake by plants. These values were all converted from µmol CO2 m-2 s-1 to g C m-2 year-1. Global warming potential (GWP) was calculated by multiplying CO2, CH4, and N2O by their respective 100-year GWP CO2-eq (i.e., 27 for CH4, 273 for N2O) following previous studies (Myhre et al. 2014; Petrakis et al. 2017; Capooci and Vargas 2022; Fettrow et al. 2023) and the updated IPCC CO2-equivelent values (IPCC 6th Assessment Report, 2020; Section 7.6.1.1). Total GWP was the sum of the CO2-eq of each GHG measured. A positive GWP indicates a net warming effect of GHGs while a negative GWP indicates a net cooling effect of GHGs. In addition, Photosynthetic Photo Flux Density (PPFD) (µmol photon m-2 s-1) was recorded in the field during sunny, partly cloudy, and cloudy conditions so that light measurements could be assigned a qualitative PPFD correction (i.e., ×1, ×1.5 and ×2 respectively). PPFD-corrected CO2 variables are reported only in Supplemental Information (SI, Figure S1), as these are qualitative, not quantitative, adjustments. In addition, we found that the semi-transparent chamber blocked 33% of incoming light, and therefore a 33% correction was accounted for when calculating NEE, GPP, and GWP assuming a linear response to light levels (Mbufong et al., 2014).
Plant/ Soil and Porewater Collection and Analysis
Following the vegetation survey, plant tissues and soils were sampled from subplots containing the dominant PFTs present at each landscape position. In the lowland, graminoids were the only dominant vascular PFT present, while in the uplands, dominant vascular PFTs included graminoids, forbs, evergreen shrubs, and deciduous shrubs. A greater number of plant and soil samples were taken from the upland to capture the greater diversity of PFTs. Aboveground vegetation and belowground root samples were sampled in select subplots based on the presence of dominant PFTs in our initial percent cover survey. We chose subplots in the upland with the greatest percent cover of graminoids, forbs, evergreen shrubs, and deciduous shrubs to represent those respective PFTs in triplicate (n = 3) for each PFT type. A 10-cm × 10-cm square surface sample was taken to 10 cm depth with plants and roots intact. Each 10-cm × 10-cm × 10-cm soil block was placed into individual Ziploc bags, put on ice in the field, and frozen (-18 °C) within 3 hours for storage until transport back to Oak Ridge National Laboratory.
In the lab, surface root cores were thawed and processed within 48 hours of thawing according to the following procedure. Aboveground vegetation (i.e., graminoid leaf blades and sheaths, forb leaves, and leaves and woody stems of shrubs) belonging to the representative PFT for that core was removed, sorted, and oven-dried at 70°C for ~72 hrs prior to being weighed. Belowground stems (rhizomes) were also removed and sorted. Fine roots were separated into two different functional classes: transport fine roots and absorptive fine roots based on root order, where the first three, most distal, root orders were considered absorptive fine roots responsible for water and nutrient acquisition (McCormack et al. 2015). Both transport (0.72 ± 0.01 mm diameter) and absorptive fine roots (0.22 ± 0.02 mm diameter) were separated, cleaned with distilled deionized water (DDI), and scanned at 1400 dpi on a flatbed scanner for determination of root length and average root diameter (WinRhizo software, Regent Instruments, Inc., Québec, Canada). Complete removal of absorptive fine roots was only possible for graminoid samples; therefore this was the only PFT for which adsorptive fine root biomass pools (0-10 cm) are reported. Roots were then dried at 70°C for ~72 hrs and weighed. Specific root length (SRL) for each root class was calculated using root length and dry mass (cm mg-1). Carbon and N content in above- and belowground tissues were quantified on an Elementar CN analyzer (Unicube TRACE, Elementar).
Separate soil cores for biogeochemical analyses were collected using a 2-inch diameter gouge auger (AMS) starting from surface soils until reaching either permafrost in the upland (< 62 cm; Table S1) or auger length (~1 meter) in the lowland plots; there were no rocks or bedrock to limit sampling depth at these sites. The cores were immediately sectioned into 10-cm increments in the field, placed into gas-impermeable bags, vacuum sealed, put on ice, then frozen until laboratory analysis. In the lab, each 10-cm increment of soil was thawed in an anoxic glove bag (98% N, 2% H) to avoid oxygen exposure. Once thawed, the field-moist 10-cm sections were placed into 250-mL centrifuge vials and capped inside the glove bag to maintain anoxic conditions inside the vial. Soils were then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 2 minutes to separate the porewater from the solid phase. Porewater was decanted and filtered (0.45 µm) and immediately measured for pH and oxidation reduction potential (ORP; ExTech RE300) referenced to a standard hydrogen electrode. Remaining porewater was aliquoted into several individual containers for analysis of dissolved organic C (DOC; solutions acidified to 2% with hydrochloric acid) and dissolved inorganic C (DIC; Shimadzu TOC analyzer), total elements (solutions acidified to 2% with trace metal grade nitric acid, Agilent, ICP-OES), Fe2+ (HACH kit, Method 8146) and EMMs-UV-VIS, (HORIBA, Aqualog).
The Aqualog was calibrated using deionized water blanks, and data were normalized to the instrument’s Raman Area. Wavelengths between 230 nm and 700 nm were measured with a measurement step of 2 nm. Fluorescence peak intensities (i.e., Coble Peaks A, C, B and T normalized by DOC concentration) and indices (FI, HIX, BIX) were determined, as well as absorbance indices (i.e., Abs254, Sr, SUVA254, E2: E3). These peaks and indices were calculated using previously published equations and their chemical characterization property meanings were inferred based on previous studies (Table 1).
If soil cores were too dry to extract porewater, lab-grade deionized water (DI) was added to the 250-mL vials inside the glove bag in a 5:1 ratio (soil:water), shaken at 300 rpm for 30 minutes, and extracted as described above. All but two lowland soils (n= 30) had enough porewater to extract without deionized water, while all upland soils (n = 56) had DI added. After centrifugation, the soil was placed back into the glove bag to air dry anoxically. Desiccant was placed inside the glove bag and frequently regenerated to rapidly dry soils. Once dry, the soils were ground and sieved to 2 mm and further powdered and homogenized with mortar and pestle. These soils were further dried at 70ºC for 72 hrs prior to weighing and combustion for total C and N (Unicube TRACE, Elementar). Furthermore, select soil samples in the glove bag were further characterized using Synchrotron techniques described below.
In addition to the porewater collected via soil core centrifugation, porewater was also collected directly in the field in locations adjacent to the 1-m × 1-m plots using porewater sipper MacroRhizons. Vacuum was applied to draw water from the MacroRhizon in the soil into a syringe, after which the syringe was removed from the tubing and the water was immediately measured in the field for specific conductance, pH, and dissolved oxygen (DO) (Mettler Toledo) using calibrated probes. The remaining porewater sample was preserved for later analysis in the lab following procedures outlined above. We, however, focus our main analysis on the soil cores (porewater and soil), but field collected porewater data are included in the SI (Table S2) for comparison.
